title: Identification of the length scale parameter of simplified strain gradient elasticity from standard Mode I fracture tests
authors: Yury Solyaev, Kirill Shelkov, Pavel Polyakov
abstract: Recently, it was shown that additional material constants of strain gradient elasticity (SGE) can be identified for brittle and quasi-brittle materials based on the analysis of experimental data on the crack size effect. In the present paper, we perform precise numerical simulations within SGE and derive regression relations for processing experimental data from standard fracture mechanics tests under pure Mode I loading conditions (CCT, SENT, SENB). We consider the simplified SGE, whose constitutive relations contain a single length scale parameter $\ell$ in addition to the classical elastic constants. We show that, for brittle materials, this parameter can be explicitly identified as $\ell \approx 0.362 (K_{Ic}/σ_{ult})^2$. This identification ensures that the fracture loads predicted by classical linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM) and by the simplified SGE coincide for relatively long Mode I cracks. However, within the simplified SGE, these fracture loads are evaluated from the nonsingular stress field using the maximum principal stress criterion. For quasi-brittle materials, we derive regression relations that describe the non-classical size effect on strength. This effect is usually treated within nonlinear fracture mechanics but can be naturally captured by SGE. Examples of identification of the length scale parameter $\ell$ based on the established relations and the experimental data for chopped fiber composites and for porous and dense quasi-brittle ceramics are presented.
summary: This paper develops a framework using simplified Strain Gradient Elasticity (SGE) to model fracture in brittle and quasi-brittle materials, incorporating the effect of material size. By performing numerical simulations on standard fracture tests, the authors successfully derive explicit and empirical relations to identify the material's characteristic length scale parameter ($\ell$). This advancement allows for a more accurate prediction of fracture loads that account for size effects beyond classical linear elastic fracture mechanics.
main_problem: The paper aims to identify the length scale parameter ($\ell$) of simplified strain gradient elasticity (SGE) by analyzing standard Mode I fracture tests.
main_result: For brittle materials, the length scale parameter is explicitly identified as $\ell \approx 0.362 (K_{Ic}/\sigma_{ult})^2$, while regression relations are derived for quasi-brittle materials to describe the non-classical size effect.
method: The authors use precise numerical simulations within the SGE framework, deriving regression relations from experimental data obtained from standard fracture mechanics tests (CCT, SENT, SENB) under pure Mode I loading.
model_or_system: The model is the simplified SGE, which extends classical elasticity by incorporating a single length scale parameter $\ell$ via higher-order strain gradient terms (double stress $\mu_{ijk}$). This is applied to brittle and quasi-brittle materials exhibiting crack size effects.
key_observables: Length scale parameter ($\ell$), fracture loads, stress and strain concentrations, and the J-integral.
important_parameters: Length scale parameter ($\ell$), fracture toughness ($K_{Ic}$), ultimate stress ($\sigma_{ult}$), and the ratio $R/l$.
main_assumptions: The simplified SGE is an approximation, and the identification of $\ell$ for brittle materials ensures load coincidence with classical LEFM only for relatively long cracks.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the FEM mesh near the crack tip using enriched elements and show convergence studies for stress components ($	au_{22}$) and fracture parameters ($K_1, K_2$) with respect to integration points and mesh density.
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical formulation of SGE, presents the numerical methodology using enriched FEM for standard fracture geometries (CCT, SENT, SENB), derives the identification relations for $\ell$, and validates these relations using both theoretical derivations and comparisons with experimental data.
